note: The estate's history as a timeline, retold in this record's own words from the concise history printed on The Park Map, Fourth Edition, by Douglas de Havilland, which he gave to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association. The facts are his; the sentences are not, because reproducing a man's own prose on a public page is a different thing from drawing on his research. The raw transcript stays in history_park_map_dougal.json, where the wording IS his, so the two can always be compared. Every entry that was once left hanging — where the map's column wrapped and the PDF's text layer lost the rest — has now been read off the original by A. Hagues and completed.
source: The Park Map, Fourth Edition, designed by Douglas de Havilland and donated to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association. Retold, not reproduced.

entries.text: Saxon settlers arrive and pass the sandstone rock by, putting their settlement instead on the ground where St Mary's church and the Lace Market stand today.

William the Conqueror, seeing the rock, orders a castle raised on it by his son Peverel. The woodland beside it is enclosed as a royal hunting ground, and that ground and the castle together are used by kings and their courts for the next four hundred years.
Nottingham receives its Great Charter, and from this point answers to nobody below the King.
Richard III is said to have mustered his troops in the Deer Park, marching them over the King's Meadow and away to Bosworth.
Charles I stays at Thurland Hall rather than the castle, which by now is reckoned unfit for a king.

Charles raises his standard on the ground now called Standard Hill. The town stays loyal to Parliament. William Cavendish backs the King heavily, with money and with men; the war ends with Charles executed in 1649.
With the war over, Colonel Willoughby has the castle pulled down, to the considerable relief of a good many Nottinghamians.
The ruin is bought by William Cavendish, made 1st Duke of Newcastle three years later for the support he gave the King in the war.
Work starts on an Italianate palace on the site, at a cost of £14,000. The Duke dies before it is finished.

Queen Anne, second daughter of James II, comes to the throne. As Princess Anne she had lived at the Mansion House. Queen Anne's Garden and Queen Anne's Chamber still carry her name at the castle, which suggests she may have been the last of the Stuarts to stay there.
The Duke leaves no male heir, and the title is recreated for his nephew Thomas Pelham, later Pelham-Holles, as 1st Duke of Newcastle.
No male heir again. The dukedom is recreated a second time, for the nephew Henry Pelham Clinton, who becomes the 2nd Duke.

The last of the great balls is held at the ducal mansion, given by the Duke — Earl of Lincoln and Colonel of the Nottingham Militia as well. The building is then let out as apartments, and in part as a boarding school.
The old castle fishponds are filled in with spoil dug out for the Cavalry Barracks going up at the north-west corner of the Park. The made ground gives allotments with a name for what they grow.
Henry Clinton dies and his son Thomas succeeds as 3rd Duke.

The 3rd Duke dies at forty-two, after a whooping cough treatment that went badly wrong. He leaves a widow of thirty-five as Dowager Duchess, and a son of ten — Henry Pelham Fiennes Pelham Clinton, the Fiennes said “fines”.
The Dowager marries again, and sells land on Standard Hill to provide for the young Duke.
The first national census puts Nottingham at close to thirty thousand people. It passes forty thousand by 1821, and fifty thousand by 1831.
The 4th Duke, twenty-two years old, marries the heiress Georgina Elizabeth Munday of Shipley in Derbyshire, and £190,000 with her.
William Stretton builds St James's Church on Standard Hill. A nurses' home will replace it in 1936.
St Mary's Vicarage goes up on Standard Hill — the first building anywhere in what was then the Park.
Regency House is built at 2 Ropewalk, and is the oldest house standing in The Park today.
The 4th Duke, who is not popular, proposes developing the Park as a residential quarter. The townspeople resent it: they regard the Park as their own ground, to walk in.
Rioters set the Duke's mansion alight, provoked by his vote against the Reform Bill.
Fifty large houses now stand around the edge of the Park, built in the face of local opposition — on Western Terrace, Park Terrace, and Ropewalk Street, now The Ropewalk.

The 4th Duke dies. His son, Lord Lincoln, is held in far better regard by the town and its council than his father ever was. As 5th Duke he puts Thomas Chambers Hine — much the ablest architect in the town — in charge of the Park's development, every house to have Hine's approval, including those of his rival Fothergill Watson.
T. C. Hine oversees the restoration of the burnt mansion. The Corporation takes the building on and opens in it the first municipal museum and art gallery in England.

Nearly four hundred houses have been built, for the most part for wealthy and influential Nottingham men: A. J. Mundella the educationalist, Sir Jesse Boot the pharmacist, Sir Albert Ball the plumber, John Player in tobacco, Thomas Foreman the printer, Sir John Jardine in lace machinery, and the Bowden, Birkin and Bayley families — bicycles, lace and leather.
Queen Victoria makes Nottingham a city, in the year of her Diamond Jubilee.
After 277 years in the family, the 8th Duke sells the Park to Oxford University, the purchase made through Lord Nuffield.
Clumber Park is sold to the National Trust. The house there had been pulled down in 1938 to raise money.

Years of work by the Park Residents' Association, with the lawyer John Hallam at the helm, bring Nottingham Park Estate Ltd into being: residents electing their own unpaid board to look after the roads, pavements, gas lamps, trees and greens. Peter Millican keeps the gas lighting.
The 10th Duke dies and the dukedom of Newcastle becomes extinct.
The estate's records are moved from Oxford to the University of Nottingham.
